data.title: Trump rips Rove: 'So bad for the Republican Party'
data.description:
President Trump blasted Republican strategist Karl Rove on Monday, calling former President George W. Bush’s White House adviser, “so bad for the Republican party.”

Rove received Trump’s ire after he said he will vote for Democrat Jon Rosenthal to serve on the Texas Railroad Commission after GOP candidate Bo French wrote a post about University of Texas at Austin (UT-Austin) students of South Asian descent, described by UT students as “blatantly racist.”

“Karl Rove is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “He suffers from a major case of Trump Derangement Syndrome primarily because, for almost 10 years, I beat back and won against so many of the people and things that he wanted and espoused.”

The president ended the post asking why Fox News and The Wall Street Journal “keep this Rino [Republican in name only] Voice alive.”

“The guy is a stone cold loser!” he added.

Rove told members at a Headliners Club lunch in Austin on Monday that he would vote for Rosenthal, adding that he last voted for a Democrat in 1994 when he backed former Texas Lt. Gov. Bob Bullock (D), The Texas Tribune reported. Three attendees told the outlet that the strategist called French a “bigot.”

French shared a photo taken of the UT students celebrating after a Texas football game and wrote in a post on social platform X that he “heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

He also shared a screenshot of another X user who captioned the photo “Bollywood University.”

UT-Austin students and U.S. citizens Dhairya Gupta and Rahul Kodali, who were both in the photo French posted, slammed French over the post in an interview with The Dallas Morning News on Monday.

“Whether or not we are immigrants, that doesn’t change anything,” Kodali told the outlet, with Gupta having immigrated at 5 years old and later obtaining his citizenship. “I’ve been an American my entire life.”

Texas Republicans slammed French and urged him to delete the post. Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R) echoed the sentiment, saying the candidate can oppose immigration policies “without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity –– this post has crossed the line.”

“This is the Republican nominee for statewide office,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) wrote online. “Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad.”

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate seeking to succeed Cornyn in November, thanked the GOP senator for condemning the post and asked if his Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, would condemn “this blatant racism.”

Paxton instead accused Talarico of having “a history of dividing Texans by race.”

data.title: SNAP benefits are changing in October: What to know
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Heads up, SNAP recipients: Your monthly benefit allotment is likely about to change.

On Oct. 1, the annual cost-of-living adjustment (or COLA) kicks in, meaning the size of most people’s SNAP benefits are about to increase slightly.

Single people, however, will only receive $8 more per month. A family of four will get $29 more monthly. That’s about a 2.9% increase in benefits.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the cost of food at home has gone up about 2.7% year-over-year. Overall inflation is at 3.4%.

Starting Oct. 1, 2026, this is how SNAP recipients in the 48 contiguous U.S. states plus D.C. will see their maximum benefits change:

Maximum benefit amounts are different in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands, due to the high cost of groceries in those places. A family of four in rural Alaska, for example, will be getting as much as $2,027 starting in October.

In Hawaii, benefits are actually decreasing slightly. A household of four in Hawaii will now have a maximum benefit of $1,655. (See more on the maximum benefits in those states and territories here.)

SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, helps about 37 million lower-income Americans buy groceries. The program — formerly known as the Food Stamps — is also changing its eligibility requirements as of October.

How much someone receives in SNAP benefits depends on their household income and assets. Generally, you qualify for at least some assistance if your gross monthly income is less than $1,729 as an individual or $3,575 as a family of four.

The asset limit will remain unchanged this year. It’s set at $3,000 for most households, or $4,750 in households where someone is disabled or 60 and older.

Work status, immigration status, age and disabilities can also impact the ability to receive food aid.

SNAP enrollment dropped more than expected over the past year as changes to the program, put forth in the Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill in 2025, started to take effect. Enrollment in the food aid program dropped by about 13% in one year.

Many states are at risk of even bigger cuts to the program in the coming years, as federal funding is now tied to error rates. As of June, only nine states were in compliance with the new standards.

data.title: Your check for $5,000 is not in the mail
data.description:
President Trump is not the first to dangle a tempting reward before people to get them to vote.

In the early 1990s, the California Democratic Party made a deal with Krispy Kreme: a free dozen donuts for anyone who walked in wearing an “I Voted” sticker. You voted, you qualified for a dozen donuts — no questions asked. I know all about it, because at that time I was chair of the state Democratic Party.

But that’s a far cry from what Trump has proposed. Unlike Trump, we didn’t offer free donuts only to those who voted Democrat, or only if Democrats won the election. And there was no cash involved.

What Trump proposed on the first night of last week’s midterm convention in Dallas is close to a pure bribe. It was like Oprah Winfrey, telling everyone in the audience to look under their seat for keys to a new Pontiac G6 — except Oprah delivered. There is no guarantee that Trump would.

“If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump promised his audience of MAGA Republicans in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.” But of course, like everything else Trump does, it comes with strings attached: “We don’t want you going to Canada to spend the money,” he said.

While Trump’s proposal may technically be legal — amounting to nothing more than another questionable campaign pledge, like promising to end the war in Ukraine on day one — it has several other problems, starting with the fact that, under the Constitution, a president cannot send money to Americans without approval by Congress. And that could prove difficult, even if Republicans do, as unlikely as it may seem, maintain control of both the House and Senate.

There are roughly 245 million adult American citizens. According to the Associated Press, giving each of them a check for $5,000 would cost the treasury $1.3 trillion — which would make it the second most expensive of all government programs. Topped only by Social Security ($1.6 trillion), but greater than Medicare ($996.7 billion), health care ($978.9 billion), interest on the national debt ($970.4 billion), and national defense ($916.6 billion).

That might prove to be a hard pill to swallow, even for loyal Trumpers. Especially after the national debt recently exploded to a gigantic $40 trillion. Which is why Trump’s $5,000 proposal received such a tepid response from prominent Republicans.

“Tying government checks to the outcome of an election starts to sound like pay-to-play politics,” sniffed Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

It will only lead to “more debt and more inflation,” predicted Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R).

“I would personally throw everything of my heart and soul to stop it,” pledged Rep. David Schweikert (R-Ariz.), “because it would actually do more damage to working people than would ever help them.”

Frequent Trump critic Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) wrote on X he was “insulted by the notion that my vote this November could be bought for $5K.”

When asked whether Senate Republicans would approve Trump’s “dividend,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) would only say: “We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it.”

But the biggest problem with Trump’s $5,000 promise is that it’s hard to take seriously. Many Americans just won’t believe him. Because he’s tried this same trick before. In early 2025, after Elon Musk announced he was going to save taxpayers $2 trillion in cuts to the federal government, he and Trump promised to send dividend checks of $5,000 to every American household. DOGE didn’t save $2 trillion, and no checks ever went out.

On Nov. 9, 2025, after launching his global tariffs, President Trump promised to “issue a dividend to our middle-income people and lower income people of about $2,000.” But Trump’s tariffs, severely curtailed by the Supreme Court, have only yielded $341 billion in income and, so far, no checks have been mailed.

Before leaving Ireland on Sunday, Trump insisted that, despite these problems, his $5,000 dividend checks were a sure bet. “One hundred percent!“

A wiser voice would say: Don’t count on it. You never got the DOGE check or the tariffs check. You’re not going to get this Republican victory check, either. It’s just one more broken Donald Trump promise.

You’d be better off going to California to vote. At least, you’d walk away with a dozen donuts.

Bill Press is host of The Bill Press Pod. He is the author of “From the Left: A Life in the Crossfire.”

data.title: Meet the wealthiest person in your state, according to latest Forbes report
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) — While you may be bogged down by the high costs of groceries and gas, the wealthy have never been wealthier, according to the latest report from Forbes.

The 400 wealthiest Americans are now worth a record $8 trillion, Forbes reported Tuesday. That’s up from the $6.6 trillion they were worth in last year’s Forbes 400.

To make the annual list at all, you need to have a net worth of $4.4 billion, also an increase over last year. Forbes said that benchmark left 590 billionaires off the list.

To be among the top 10, you needed far, far more. Nebraska’s Warren Buffett ranked as No. 10 overall on the Forbes 400 list for 2026 with an estimated net worth of $144 billion.

Unsurprisingly, Elon Musk, who was briefly the world’s first trillionaire, again ranked at No. 1 overall with an estimated net worth of $908 billion, according to Forbes.

Twelve states – Alabama, Alaska, Delaware, Idaho, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, North Dakota, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Vermont, and West Virginia – were not represented on this year’s Forbes 400.

The interactive table below details the wealthiest resident in the remaining states and the District of Columbia, per Forbes’ rankings:

In total, 62 women ranked within the Forbes 400, the same as last year. The wealthiest among them remains Alice Walton, the only daughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton. With an estimated net worth of $118 billion, she ranks as the third-wealthiest Texan and the 13th wealthiest American.

Walton falls well behind Texas’ wealthiest resident, Musk, keeping her off the table above. You will, however, find Kentucky’s Tamara Gustavson, Maryland’s Annette Lerner and her family, Massachusetts’ Abigail Johnson, Nevada’s Miriam Adelson and her family, Virginia’s Jacqueline Mars, and Wisconsin’s Diane Hendricks.

Three states – California, Georgia and Ohio – have a new wealthiest resident. In California, Google’s Larry Page replaced Oracle’s Larry Ellison, who moved to Florida. Home Depot’s Arthur Blank beat out the children of Truett Cathy, the founder of Chick-fil-A, to rank as the wealthiest resident of Georgia. Denise York and her family, who own the San Francisco 49ers, edged out Les Wexner and his family, who are responsible for Victoria’s Secret and Bath & Body Works, in Ohio.

President Donald Trump again made the list, but with a slight drop in his net worth to an estimated $7 billion, down from $7.3 billion last year. The dip, while small, was enough to drop him from No. 201 to No. 245.

You can view Forbes’ latest rankings here.

Thirty-four people who made the rankings last year failed to do so this year, including Roblox cofounder David Baszucki.

data.title: Trump approval ticks up from record low: Survey
data.description:
President Trump’s approval rating has risen slightly after hitting a record low last month, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll released weeks before the midterm elections.

Thirty-five percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance as the deeply unpopular Iran war reached its sixth month, up from 33 percent in a late August poll revealing his lowest rating across both of his terms.

The poll also revealed growing popularity for Democrats among Americans, as Democrats held a 7-point advantage over Republicans when U.S. voters were asked which party they would support if the elections were held today. Forty-four percent chose Democrats and 37 percent preferred Republicans.

The survey was conducted in the days after Republicans gathered in Dallas for the party’s midterm convention, where Trump sought to rally voters around keeping GOP control of the House and Senate.

Trump’s pledge that he made at the convention to provide Americans with $5,000 dividend checks if Republicans maintain control of Congress received little support in the poll, with 63 percent of Americans saying they disapproved of it — including 4 in 10 Republicans and 9 in 10 Democrats.

Trump has since defended the proposed payments, which could add more than $1 trillion to the national debt and would likely require approval from Congress.

The proposal fell flat with fiscal hawks in the GOP, who said they would not support handing out money to people who do not work or pay taxes.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey also showed a shift toward Democrats on the economy, an issue that has become central amid rising inflation and trade disruptions from the Iran war that have caused oil and gas prices to surge.

Thirty-eight percent of respondents said Democrats would do a better job handling the economy, compared with 37 percent who sided with Republicans. Reuters reported Democrats gained an advantage on the issue over the summer for the first time in about a decade.

data.title: Watch live: House Democrats speak amid AI, affordability battle
data.description:
House Democratic leaders will speak with reporters Tuesday morning as Democrats pressure the Trump administration for more regulations on artificial intelligence and experts warn of increasing risks.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has emerged as one of the loudest critics of the rapidly evolving technology, calling on his colleagues to pass legislation enacting new guardrails on the AI industry. His upper chamber counterpart, Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), also pressed for more transparency as Republican leaders and President Trump brush off the anxieties.

Meanwhile, with the midterms less than two months away, Democrats have centered much of their messaging on the affordability crisis tied to Trump’s war with Iran as the party looks to take control of Congress next year.

The event is scheduled to begin at 11:30 a.m. EDT.

data.title: Trump rips justices on mail-in ballots: 'These are not the people I interviewed to serve'
data.description:
President Trump on Tuesday slammed the Supreme Court ruling that upheld the block on his mail-in voting plan, singling out the conservative justices who ruled with the majority.

Trump referred to the ruling, which upheld a judge’s block finding the plan unlawful, as “a bad decision” in a lengthy TruthSocial post. 

The president praised conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas as “legends,” noting their dissent against the ruling. However, he lashed out at “certain” other justices who “are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats,” apparently referring to Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett, who sided with liberals on the ruling.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United  States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal,” the president wrote. 

Trump went on to predict the high court will go down as having “rendered some of the most destructive, hurtful, and damaging decisions in our Country’s history.” 

While he voted with the majority, Kavanaugh suggested there’s at least a fair prospect that the plan is legal. 

“But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections,” Kavanaugh wrote.

The decision marks the third time the Trump administration brought the plan to the high court’s emergency docket after groups blocked the effort.  

The plan would have directed states to upload voter lists before sending out mail-in ballots. Additionally, the Postal Service would only deliver ballots that meet new design requirements. 

“Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court, one that the Court System took forever to give, and then blamed it, in part, on no time left to implement a solution to our totally CORRUPT and out of control Mail-In voting ‘disaster,’ which is a laughing stock all over the World, and where we are the only country that has to endure such a Nation Destroying SCAM,” Trump wrote in his post.

data.title: NBC boosts security at 'Today' studio after string of incidents: Report
data.description:
(NewsNation) — NBC has increased security at the “Today” show’s Manhattan studio following several incidents, including an encounter involving a co-host and the unsolved abduction of co-host Savannah Guthrie’s mother from her Arizona home.

Page Six first reported the changes, citing unnamed insiders who said the safety updates were long overdue but have made staffers feel safer.

“It was much needed and took longer than people would have liked, but it does feel a lot better now,” one insider told the outlet.

Another source said “Today” staffers have been willing to follow the new protocols, despite the added security measures being more burdensome. NBC has not publicly detailed all of the new security measures.

The changes follow a July incident in which police arrested an intruder who allegedly accessed a secure area near the “Today” studio.

Later that month, Variety obtained an internal memo outlining some of the planned changes. NBC sources confirmed the memo was authentic.

One change limits guests to two accompanying people, including stylists, publicists, social media aides and other support personnel.

The July incident involved 41-year-old Andrew Truelove, who allegedly slipped past security and entered an area outside the “Today” studio. According to police, Truelove confronted Craig Melvin and asked where he could find Al Roker before allegedly directing a racial slur at Melvin.

Melvin alerted security, and Truelove was arrested. A security guard was reportedly fired following the incident.

Truelove faces charges including felony burglary and misdemeanor menacing in connection with the incident.

Court records show a man with the same name and age also has other pending cases in New York, including allegations involving an assault, trespassing and reckless endangerment on the city’s transit system as well as a 12-count criminal mischief indictment from last year.

The security changes come months after Guthrie’s mother, Nancy, was abducted from her home in Tucson, Ariz., on Feb. 1. She has not been found.

While the incidents are separate, the combination of the unsolved abduction and multiple security breaches has heightened concerns among “Today” staffers.

The latest changes at NBC’s 30 Rockefeller Center are intended to strengthen security for employees, guests and visitors to the studio.

data.title: Study links cats to more anxiety, behavioral issues in young kids
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Got a cat and a toddler in the house? One study suggests that could lead to a purrrfect storm when it comes to your child’s emotional development.

Researchers tracking nearly 1,900 families found kids who had a cat at home, specifically kids aged 4-5, were more likely to show signs of anxiety, withdrawal or emotional struggles by the time they turned 7 or 8.

They were also somewhat more likely to act out, break rules or have other behavioral issues.

The study also looked at dogs, birds, rodents, fish and reptiles, but none showed the same pattern.

So, what’s the deal with cats?

According to a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics last year, kids who had a cat between ages 4 and 5 were about 37 percent more likely to show “internalizing” problems, like worry, sadness and emotional distancing. They were also around 27 percent more likely to show “externalizing problems, like acting out or showing difficulty with impulse control.

Researchers give a few possible explanations for this. The first: Cats tend to be lower-maintenance and less interactive than dogs, so kids may get less important outdoor play and social engagement time.

They also theorize that families who already have a child dealing with stress or behavioral challenges might specifically choose to own a cat because it’s easier to manage — meaning cats may not be the reason for the behavior at all, but simply along for the ride.

One even wilder theory: Some cats can carry a parasite called toxoplasmosis, which has been linked to psychiatric disorders, including bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, according to past research. The parasite is usually picked up from raw meat or outdoor hunting, then shed in litter box waste. The 2025 study was observational only and did not test any children or cats for the parasite.

Should parents be wary of cats in the home?

Researchers say the study is a correlation and does not determine that cats cause anxiety.

Several other factors can play a role in a child’s emotional development and behavior.

Parents can watch their young children for signs of increased clinginess or worry, trouble sleeping, withdrawing from friends or family or frequent meltdowns, but none of these behaviors are unique to households with cats.

data.title: Trump wants a referendum on Trump ahead of the midterms — let's give him one.
data.description:
The strangest thing about last week’s Republican convention in Dallas wasn’t that Donald Trump managed to turn a midterm election into something resembling another presidential campaign. It was that so many people immediately began arguing about the spectacle. 

Was this normal? Was it appropriate? Was it another example of a political party organizing itself around one man? What did it say about the Republican Party? What did it say about Trump? 

At one point, Trump asked the audience to raise their right hands and pledge themselves to the “greatest president in the history of the United States” and to voting in November. Then, with his own hand raised, he declared: “I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.” 

It was weird. It was cringy. It was wildly inappropriate. And a sitting president joking about cheating in an election after years of making unsupported claims that his opponents do exactly that deserves criticism. 

But it also illustrates something exhausting about American politics in the Trump era. Every provocation becomes the story. Every norm-breaking moment generates several days of outrage, defense and counter-outrage. Then another one arrives. 

In Dallas, Trump actually offered Americans a much more useful way to judge him. He told voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” 

OK. Let’s do exactly that. 

Trump has spent most of his adult life asking to be judged as an executive. So let’s borrow an executive term and look, as impartially and dispassionately as possible, at his key performance indicators. 

Trump’s approval rating now stands at 33 percent in the Reuters/Ipsos poll, the lowest level of his political career. He began his second term at 47 percent. Among independents, the numbers are particularly ugly. Heading into an election Trump has explicitly asked voters to make about him, independents currently prefer Democratic congressional candidates 36 percent to 22 percent.

Approval ratings are snapshots, of course; they are not history’s final verdict on a presidency. But they are certainly a KPI. So is the economy. 

Trump returned to office in no small part because Americans were angry about affordability. Today, 71 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, including four in 10 Republicans.

Has the economy has collapsed? No. And there are areas of genuine strength for Trump; the border is unquestionably quieter than it was when he returned to office, and that is a KPI on which he deserves substantial credit. 

That is what a dispassionate review requires. Count the wins. Count the losses. Do not move the goalposts for either. Then look overseas. 

Trump ran as the president who would keep America out of prolonged wars. The United States is now in the seventh month of a war with Iran, with no immediate end in sight. The Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted. Energy prices have risen. The conflict has threatened to widen again through Yemen and another crucial shipping passage, at Bab el-Mandeb. 

There may be legitimate arguments for confronting Iran. History may ultimately judge some of Trump’s decisions more favorably than voters do today. But that is not the KPI Trump originally offered. He promised something considerably simpler: strength would produce peace. 

Which brings us to Ukraine. 

Trump spent years saying Russia’s invasion would never have happened had he been president. More importantly, he repeatedly claimed that his negotiating ability could end the war extraordinarily quickly. At times he talked about doing it within 24 hours, even before taking office. 

He has now been president for nearly 20 months. The war continues. 

American negotiators are still attempting to broker a settlement. Russia and Ukraine remain divided on fundamental issues. Ukrainians are preparing for another winter of Russian attacks. 

There may be no American president capable of quickly resolving a conflict in which Vladimir Putin and Ukraine want fundamentally incompatible things. But that is precisely why the original promise matters. Trump did not campaign on the proposition that Ukraine was an extraordinarily difficult geopolitical problem requiring patience, compromise and years of diplomacy. He campaigned on the proposition that he could solve it, fast. 

And that is the useful thing about applying KPIs to Trump. We do not even have to devise the metrics ourselves because, for years, Trump himself has supplied them. 

Wars would end. Prices would fall. America would become more prosperous. Adversaries would respond to strength. His negotiating ability would succeed where traditional diplomacy had failed.

Some of those promises have produced results. Others plainly have not. 

Which brings us back to Dallas. 

Trump wants Americans to pretend he is on the ballot in November. They should. Not because they adore him. Not because they despise him. And certainly not because of another week of arguments over whether his latest convention performance was normal. 

Open the dashboard instead. Look at the promises. Look at the numbers. Look at the world Trump inherited and the world nearly two years of his presidency has produced. Then think about who should win in November’s elections.

Aron Solomon is chief strategy officer for AMPLIFY and has taught entrepreneurship at McGill University and the University of Pennsylvania.
